# The Coastline Problem, and Other Things Maps Leave Out

Measure the coast of Britain and you will get a different answer depending on how you measure it. Use a ruler a hundred kilometers long and you skip over the small bays, the estuaries, the shingle spits, and the rocky fingers that jut into the sea. The total comes out shorter. Shrink the ruler to ten kilometers and it bends into more of the detail, and the total grows. Shrink it to one kilometer, then to a hundred meters, then to the length of a boot, and the coastline keeps getting longer. Each finer measurement reveals inlets that the coarser one could not see. In the limit, the coast has no definite length at all.

Lewis Fry Richardson, a meteorologist and pacifist who was also an odd and original thinker about conflict, noticed this in the 1950s while studying the borders of countries. Benoit Mandelbrot later gave the problem a name and a theory, and it became the starting point for fractal geometry. But the observation is older than either man, and it does not require any mathematics to feel. Stand on a beach and you know that the line between land and water is not a line at all. It is a negotiation, a fringe, a zone of wet sand and tangled kelp that moves with every tide.

I keep returning to this puzzle because it exposes something about maps in general. A map is a decision about what to keep. Every map is a compression, and compression always means loss. The cartographer must choose a scale, and the scale determines which details survive. A road atlas drops the footpaths. A nautical chart drops the farmhouses but keeps the shoals. A map of a city for tourists shows the cathedral and the river and omits the three-story laundromat where the old men play chess in the afternoons. None of these choices is wrong. They are the price of being useful. But they also mean that a map is never a neutral picture of the world. It is an argument about what matters.

---

Consider the history of maps as a history of changing priorities. Early European world maps, the mappae mundi of the medieval period, were not concerned with accurate distances. Jerusalem sat at the center, and the shape of the known world was arranged according to theology more than geography. Monsters and marvels filled the blank edges. Sometimes the cartographers wrote in the margins that beyond this point lay unknown lands full of dangers, and sometimes they simply left the parchment empty or decorated it with a sea serpent. We look at these maps and smile at their confusion, but they were honest in a way that many modern maps are not. They showed what their makers believed was important, and they did not pretend to be a mirror.

The modern map aspires to be a mirror. It uses projections, datums, and coordinate systems to pretend that the spherical Earth can be flattened without distortion. This cannot be done. Any flat representation of a globe must sacrifice something: area, shape, distance, or direction. The Mercator projection, which made navigation easier by keeping lines of constant compass bearing straight, inflates Greenland until it looks roughly as large as Africa, when in fact Africa is about fourteen times bigger. Schoolchildren who grew up with that map carried a quiet falsehood in their heads for generations. The falsehood was not malicious. It was simply the cost of a particular purpose, and the purpose was getting ships across oceans without the navigator needing trigonometry at every turn.

What interests me is that we rarely remember the sacrifice. We see the map and believe the map. The lines look authoritative. The colors look objective. A surveyed boundary feels like a fact of nature rather than the result of a dispute settled in an office, sometimes by men who had never visited the land they were dividing. Richardson's coastline paradox has a political cousin: the length of a border depends on the scale at which people agree to look at it, and borders are usually drawn with a ruler at a scale no one lives at.

---

There is a second kind of omission that interests me more, and it is the one that happens in the mind rather than on the page. Most of us carry around maps of our own lives, and these maps are compressed in the same way. We remember the big events and the landmarks: the wedding, the move to a new city, the year of the illness, the job we left. Between these points lies an enormous amount of unrecorded territory. Ordinary Tuesdays. The walk to the bus stop. The particular way a friend laughed at something stupid in a parking lot in 2009. These things are the fine-grained coastline of experience, and most of them vanish when we compress our memories into stories.

Oddly, we often feel the loss most when we return to a place we once knew well. You drive back to the town where you grew up and the road is the same but the shop on the corner is gone, replaced by something with a different name. Your memory had reduced the town to a few streets and a feeling, and now the detail has come back, unfamiliar and insistent. The town was never the map you carried. It was always the finer, longer, messier thing, and the map was a small mercy that let you live without remembering everything at once.

I think this is why nostalgia has such a strange texture. It is nostalgia for detail that we did not know we were losing. We remember the outline and forget the grain, and then we are stunned to discover how much grain there was. Proust understood this when he wrote about the madeleine dipped in tea, which dissolved a whole childhood into a single taste. The taste was a kind of key that unlocked compressed territory. The entire village of Combray came back, not as a map but as a fractal, every corner revealing another corner.

---

If maps always omit, then the question becomes how to live with that omission gracefully. One answer is to remember that the map is not the territory, which is a line so often repeated that it has become a cliché. But clichés persist because they point at something true and difficult. The map is useful precisely because it is not the territory. You cannot drive from Lisbon to Porto using a map at a one-to-one scale; the map would be as large as the country and as useless as the country itself. Abstraction is a tool, and tools are good. The trouble comes only when we forget that we made the abstraction and begin to take its outlines for the real shape of things.

Another answer is to go looking for the fine grain deliberately. Walk the coast rather than driving past it. Stop at the tide pool. Learn the names of the birds that live in the reeds at the edge of the lake. Most of us will never map a coastline or a continent, but we can practice a kind of attention that refuses to accept the first simplification. When you slow down, the world stops being a diagram and becomes a place with a texture you cannot fully summarize. A single hillside in late autumn can contain more information than any atlas. The moss on the north side of a stone, the way the light falls through a row of birches, the small bright beetle walking across a leaf: none of this will ever appear on a map, and none of it is trivial.

I find this practice steadying, perhaps because it reminds me that the world is larger than any of the representations I use to think about it. It is a kind of humility that does not require giving up on knowledge. We still need maps. We still need to summarize, to generalize, to say that a river runs from the mountains to the sea. But we can hold those summaries loosely, aware that behind each one lies a coastline that keeps growing as we look closer.

---

There is also an ethical dimension to what maps omit, and it is worth taking seriously. Whoever decides what appears on a map is exercising a kind of power. Colonial maps often erased existing place names and replaced them with the names of the surveyors' patrons. Some regions appeared as empty because no one who drew the maps bothered to ask who lived there. Indigenous communities have spent decades working to get their own place names, territorial claims, and knowledge recognized on official maps, and in many cases the fight is still ongoing. A blank space on a map is rarely blank to the people who live in it. It is blank only to the person holding the pen.

This matters for everyday life too. Digital maps now guide most of our movements, and they are remarkably good at what they do. But they also shape what we notice. A navigation app optimizes for efficiency, which means it routes us along the fastest path, past the places that are most convenient for traffic and least likely to surprise us. Over time, we may find that we have stopped wandering. We know how to get from A to B without knowing anything about the neighborhoods in between. The map has made the territory invisible. I do not think this is a catastrophe, but I think it is a loss worth naming, the way one might mention the disappearance of a species from a forest that still looks green from the highway.

Perhaps the healthiest relationship with maps is a kind of playful skepticism. Look at a map and ask what it has chosen to show. Who made it, and for what purpose? What would it look like at a different scale? Which place is missing, and why? These questions turn a passive viewing into an active reading. They also make the map more interesting, because it becomes a document of human choices rather than an oracle.

---

I want to end somewhere less analytical, because the coastline keeps reminding me that there is joy in the irreducible. Richardson's paradox is, at bottom, a delightful fact. A coastline is infinitely complicated, and no ruler can capture it. This is not a failure of measurement. It is a sign that the world has more structure than our instruments were designed to hold. Mandelbrot later showed that the same kind of self-similar complexity appears in clouds, mountains, river networks, the branching of trees, the veins of a leaf, and even the arrangement of blood vessels in the body. The rough edge repeats at every scale. Zoom in and you find the same kind of ruggedness you saw from farther away.

There is something consoling in this. It suggests that the world does not run out. However closely we look, there is more to see, and the seeing does not exhaust the thing. A map can only give you a finite number of points, but the territory keeps offering new ones. Each time you return to a familiar beach, the tide has rearranged the sand, a different piece of driftwood has washed up, and the water has gone out farther than it did last week. The coast is always being redrawn, and that redrawing is not a defect of the coast. It is what coasts do.

So I think the lesson of the coastline is not that maps are bad. It is that they are a beginning. They give us a way into a place, a rough sketch that lets us find our way, and then the place takes over and surprises us. The map gets us to the shore. The shore does the rest. We walk along the edge of the water, noticing the things no one thought to draw, and we discover that the line between land and sea is less a boundary than an invitation. It asks us to come closer, and then closer still, and it never quite finishes telling us what it is.
